                        OCCIDENTAL PERMIAN LTD.’S INITIAL BRIEF

                                          I.       INTRODUCTION

       On July 28, 2026, the Hearing Examiners issued an Order on Post-Hearing Briefing

directing SPS and Staff, and permitting other parties, to address certain issues raised at the

evidentiary hearing. 1 Specifically, the Order identified three categories of issues for briefing: (A)

any matter raised at the evidentiary hearing; (B) a recommended methodology to ensure that

production tax credits (“PTCs”) accrued in a deferred tax asset (“DTA”) do not carry forward for

an unreasonable amount of time; and (C) whether the “Energy-at-Source” allocation of PTCs is

fair to all of SPS’s rate classes, in light of the fact that some classes pay higher per-kWh rates. 2

       Occidental Permian Ltd. (“OPL”) OPL was a signatory to the Comprehensive Stipulation

filed on June 22, 2026 (the “Stipulation”), which was the product of extensive negotiations and

compromise between Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) and every party that

represents the interests of SPS’s customers, with the exception of NMPRC Staff. As discussed

further below, the Stipulation represents a represents a fair, just, and reasonable resolution of the




       1
           Order on Post-Hearing Briefing at 1-2 (July 28, 2026).
       2
           Id.

                                                         1
 matters at issue in this proceeding, and it resolves the concerns that OPL’s witnesses presented in

their testimony. The Commission should approve and adopt that Stipulation in all respects.

        With respect to Issue B, the Commission should limit the length of time that SPS may

accrue carrying charges on PTCs held in a DTA to one year from the date the credits are generated.

SPS has previously estimated that it takes an average of only 180 days to sell its PTCs after

generation, 3 so a one-year period would give SPS ample time to use or transfer its credits while

ensuring that customers do not bear carrying costs on PTCs that remain in a DTA for an

unreasonable amount of time. No similar limitation is needed for the wind PTCs generated by the

Hale and Sagamore projects before the adoption of the Inflation Reduction Act, because SPS

removed the associated DTA from the Future Test Year and customers are not paying any carrying

costs while SPS holds those credits.

        With respect to Issue C, the energy-at-source allocation of PTCs reflected in the Stipulation

is fair to all of SPS’s rate classes and should be approved. PTCs are earned in direct proportion to

the energy generated by qualifying renewable facilities, so allocating their value on an energy basis

preserves a direct, logical connection between how the credits are created and how their value

flows back to customers, consistent with cost-causation principles. Although some classes, such

as Residential, pay higher total per-kWh rates, that difference is a product of rate design: for classes

that do not have separate demand meters, demand-related costs are recovered through a premium

on the energy rate rather than through a separate demand charge. It does not reflect any difference

in the energy-related costs that each class causes SPS to incur in order to generate energy and, by

 extension, PTCs. Allocating PTC benefits on any other basis would credit certain classes for

demand-related costs that PTCs do not offset, resulting in an unwarranted cross-subsidy among

classes.

                                 II.      ARGUMENT AND AUTHORITIES

         A.           The Commission should approve the Stipulation in its entirety. [Order on
                      Post-Hearing Briefing – Issue A]

         The Stipulation that was the subject of the hearing on the merits was the product of

extensive negotiations between its signatories, which included SPS and every representative of

SPS’s customers except for the NMPRC Staff. Approving the Stipulation would result in a fair,

just, and reasonable resolution of the issues in this case, including all of the issues raised in OPL’s

direct testimony. 4

         The Stipulation addresses OPL’s concerns with SPS’s requested revenue requirement in

the following ways:

         •         The Stipulation would result in a $90.0 million revenue increase, which is significantly

                   below the $175.3 million originally requested by SPS. 5 This rate increase will allow

                   SPS to continue providing safe and reliable electric service while moderating cost

                   impacts on SPS’s customers. 6

        •      The Stipulation authorizes SPS to earn a return on equity (ROE) of 9.5%, 7 which is

              significantly below SPS’s requested 10.5% ROE. 8

       •      The Stipulation addresses OPL’s concerns regarding the rate at which SPS will earn a

              return on the deferred tax asset (DTA) associated with solar production tax credits

              (PTCs). 9 Under the terms of the Stipulation, SPS will be permitted to earn return on

              that DTA at its cost of long-term debt, which is a reasonable compromise between

              SPS’s original proposal to use its weighted average cost of capital and OPL’s

              recommendation to use SPS’s cost of short-term debt. 10

       •      The Stipulation requires SPS to amortize the investment tax credits (ITCs) associated

              with SPS’s battery energy storage systems (BESSs) over five years, which will

              significantly reduce SPS’s revenue requirement over that time frame.

       •      The Stipulation authorizes SPS to recover previously approved regulatory assets and

              fixed deferrals for excess liability insurance (ELI) premiums, investment in legacy

              meters, and Community Solar Program costs, and in exchange, SPS agreed to withdraw

              its requests to establish a property tax tracker and continue its ELI expense tracker. 11

       The Stipulation addresses OPL’s concerns with SPS’s proposed class cost/revenue

allocation in the following ways:

       The Stipulation addresses OPL’s concerns with SPS’s proposed rate design in the

following ways:

       •      SPS agreed to withdraw its request to recover prospective SPP deficiency payments

              through its FPPCAC. Instead, to the extent SPS incurs costs for deficiency payments

              (or for short-term capacity purchases to meet its capacity needs) it will defer up to $10

              million of those costs in a regulatory asset for which it may seek cost recovery in a

              future proceeding. 22 This is a reasonable result that balances SPS’s interests with those

              of its customers.

       •      The Stipulation allows SPS to retain off-system sales margins from the Cunningham

              and Plant X Solar Projects and the Cunningham 1 BESS from the commercial operation

              date of those plants until SPS is able to add the cost of those facilities into its customers’

              rates. 23 After cost recovery for those projects from customers begins, SPS will credit

              customers with all off-system sales margins, consistent with OPL’s recommendation.24

       Taken as a whole, the Stipulation represents a reasonable, negotiated resolution of the

issues presented in this proceeding, and of the issues raised by OPL in particular. As such, the

Commission should approve the Stipulation.

         B.         SPS should only be allowed to earn a return on production tax credits
                   accrued in a deferred tax asset for up to 365 days. [Order on Post-Hearing
                   Briefing – Issue B]

        The Order on Post-Hearing Briefing asks parties to recommend a methodology to ensure

that PTCs that SPS accrues in a deferred tax asset (DTA) do not carry forward for an unreasonable

amount of time. OPL believes that it would be reasonable to establish a 365-day time frame for

SPS to either use or transfer new PTCs after they are generated, and after one year, SPS would no

longer be allowed to accrue carrying charges on any remaining balance. One year should provide

adequate time for SPS to either use or transfer its PTCs. In fact, in SPS’s last FPPCAC proceeding

(Case No. 24-00270-UT), SPS witness Brooke Trammell indicated that SPS assumed an “average

annual PTC Turnover Rate of 0.49315 which represents an average of 180 days divided by 365

days in the year. This is the average estimated time that SPS expects to sell the PTCs after

generation.” 25 Given that SPS expects that it will take an average of 180 days to sell PTCs,

allowing it to accrue carrying charges for a full year should provide it with ample time to find a

buyer and complete the transfer of any PTCs that it is unable to use.

        In response to the Hearings Examiners’ subsidiary question, 26 there is no need for the

methodology above to account for wind PTCs generated by the Hale and Sagamore projects prior

to the adoption of the Inflation Reduction Act (credits earned 2019-2022) because SPS removed

the associated DTA from the Future Test Year and does not include a return on that DTA in rates,

consistent with the Final Order in Case No. 17-00044-UT. As a result, ratepayers are not currently

bearing carrying costs for SPS continuing to hold those credits. As SPS applies these credits

 against its future tax liabilities, the DTA will decline over time without cost to customers.27

Because customers are not currently bearing carrying costs on the pre-IRA wind PTC DTA (as

confirmed by SPS's removal of the DTA from the Future Test Year), there is no need to take any

steps to limit that carry-forward at this time.

         C.          The Commission should approve the Stipulation’s energy-at-source
                     allocation for PTCs because it is fair to all of SPS’s customers and consistent
                     with cost-causation principles. [Order on Post-Hearing Briefing – Issue C]

         Section 1.11 of the Stipulation provides that the value of the production tax credits

(“PTCs”) from SPS’s renewable generation will be allocated on an energy basis, 28 meaning that

SPS will flow the value of the PTCs it generates back to each customer class in direct proportion

to the amount of energy that SPS generates to serve that class. 29 This allocation methodology is

fair and reasonable, and should be approved. The fundamental justification for allocating PTCs

on an energy basis is straightforward: PTCs are created in direct proportion to the energy generated

by qualifying renewable generation facilities. 30 Accordingly, an energy allocation aligns with cost

causation principles because it maintains a direct, logical connection between how PTCs are

created (by SPS generating renewable kWh) and how the PTCs’ value is funneled back to

customers (based on the amount of renewable kWh the customer causes SPS to generate). Just as

the costs of fuel and purchased power are properly allocated on an energy basis because they vary

with energy production, PTC benefits should be allocated on an energy basis because they are

earned as a function of energy production. A class that consumes more energy causes a greater

being sold; only pre-2023 credits are carried forward).
         28

         29

         30

resource and are therefore an energy-related cost.”).

                                                            8
 need for generation, which in turn generates more PTCs. That class should therefore receive a

proportionally larger share of the PTC benefit.

        The Order on Post-Hearing Briefing directs parties to address whether Energy-at-Source

allocation is fair in light of the different prices per kWh paid by different rate classes. 31 And it is.

While it is true that some customer classes, like Residential, pay a higher rate per-kWh consumed,

that is because unlike the large commercial and industrial classes, Residential customers do not

have a separate demand meter and do not pay a separate demand charge. 32 As a result, the

Residential class’s demand-related costs—which reflect the distribution and transmission

infrastructure needed to serve peak loads—are recovered by adding a premium on top of each kWh

a residential customer consumes. Put differently, the “per-kW” rate for residential customers is

not just paying for the energy in that kW, it is also paying for a share of the

transmission/distribution capacity necessary to deliver that energy. As SPS witness Mr. Hurt

explained at the hearing, residential energy rates appear higher on a per-kWh basis because “there

is a lot of Capacity costs that make up that Energy Rate.” 33 In contrast, large commercial and

industrial customers (served at Primary and LGS-T voltage levels) typically have demand meters

and pay separate demand charges on top of their per-kWh energy rate. Their energy rates are

lower on a per-kWh basis because the demand/capacity cost component is recovered separately

through the demand charge, not bundled into the energy rate. The difference in total per-kWh

rates is attributable to the rate design used to recover demand costs, not to any difference in the



        31
             Order on Post-Hearing Briefing at 2.
        32
             Tr. Vol. II at 381:15-383:10 (Hurt).
        33

                                                    9
 underlying cost that each customer class causes SPS to incur in order to generate energy (and, by

extension, PTCs). If PTCs were instead allocated proportionally to each class’s total per-kWh

rates (including embedded demand costs in the Residential rate), the allocation would effectively

credit residential customers for demand-related costs that PTCs do not offset. This would amount

to a cross-subsidy, allocating PTC benefits to offset costs (demand/capacity costs) that are entirely

unrelated to energy production and PTC generation. It is therefore appropriate and fair to distribute

PTC benefits in the same manner as the energy costs they offset: on a per-kWh (energy) basis.

                                     III.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons discussed above, the Commission should (1) approve the Stipulation in its

entirety, including the use of energy-at-source to allocate the value of PTCs, and (2) establish a

one-year limit for SPS to accrue carrying charges on new PTCs accrued in a DTA.
